python.title: Python
python.description: A practical introduction to core Python programming, from control flow to small projects.

modules.title: Conditional Statements
modules.description: Make programs choose what to do using Boolean conditions and branching.
notes: An if statement runs its indented block only when its condition evaluates to True. Use elif for another condition and else for the fallback; indentation defines each block.
Comparisons such as ==, !=, <, and >= produce Boolean values. Use == to compare values and = to assign a value; they are not interchangeable.
Combine conditions with and, or, and not. Keep related tests readable, and remember that Python evaluates and/or with short-circuit behavior.
takeaways: Use if/elif/else to express mutually exclusive paths clearly.
Conditions must evaluate to a truth value; comparisons are a common way to create one.
Consistent indentation is part of Python syntax.

modules.title: Loops
modules.description: Repeat work with for and while loops, and control repetition safely.
notes: A for loop visits items in an iterable, such as a list or range. range( stop ) generates integers beginning at zero and excluding stop.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. Update the state used by the condition so the loop can eventually finish.
break exits the nearest loop and continue skips to its next iteration. Use these sparingly when a simple loop condition is clearer.
modules.code:
total = 0
for number in range(1, 5):
    total += number
print(total)
takeaways: Use for when iterating over a known sequence or iterable.
Use while when repetition depends on a condition that changes.
Check loop bounds carefully; range excludes its ending value.

modules.title: Strings
modules.description: Work with text using indexing, methods, formatting, and careful assumptions about characters.
notes: Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode text. Indexing starts at zero, negative indices count from the end, and slicing uses a start-inclusive, end-exclusive range.
Methods such as strip(), lower(), and replace() return new strings rather than changing the original. Method calls can be chained when each step is clear.
f-strings insert values into text using expressions in braces. Text input often needs validation and normalization; lowercasing is not a substitute for every language-aware comparison.
takeaways: String operations create results; they do not mutate the original string.
Use slicing and indexing with awareness of zero-based, end-exclusive positions.
f-strings are a readable way to combine text and values.

modules.title: Data Structures
modules.description: Choose lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets to organize collections of values.
notes: Lists are ordered and mutable, making them useful for collections that change. Tuples are ordered but immutable, and can represent a fixed grouping of values.
Dictionaries map unique, hashable keys to values. Access a key with square brackets when it must exist, or use get() when a missing key should have a default.
Sets hold distinct hashable elements and support operations such as union and intersection. Their iteration order should not be used as a meaningful sequence.
modules.code:
scores = {"Mina": 8, "Lee": 9}
scores["Mina"] += 1
unique_tags = set(["python", "data", "python"])
print(scores["Mina"], len(unique_tags))
takeaways: Select a structure based on whether order, mutation, uniqueness, or key-based lookup matters.
Dictionary keys must be unique, and missing-key behavior should be handled intentionally.
A set removes duplicates but is not an ordered list.

modules.title: Functions
modules.description: Package reusable logic into functions with parameters, return values, and clear scope.
notes: Define a function with def, give its inputs as parameters, and use return to send a result back to the caller. A function that reaches its end without returning a value returns None.
Default parameter values are evaluated once when the function is defined. Avoid mutable defaults such as [] when each call should get a fresh collection.
Local names belong to a function's local scope. Prefer passing inputs and returning outputs over relying on global state, which makes code easier to test.
modules.code:
def area_rectangle(width, height):
    return width * height

area = area_rectangle(3, 4)
print(area)
takeaways: Functions make repeated behavior reusable and easier to test.
Use return for a computed result; print is for displaying a result.
Pass needed data explicitly rather than depending on hidden global state.

modules.title: Object-Oriented Programming
modules.description: Model related data and behavior with classes and objects.
notes: A class defines a kind of object; an instance is one object created from that class. The initializer __init__ commonly assigns instance attributes through self.
Instance methods receive the instance as their first parameter, conventionally named self. Each instance can hold its own attribute values.
Use a class when a concept has related state and behavior. For a small collection of unrelated values or a simple transformation, a function or built-in data structure may be simpler.
takeaways: Classes describe shared structure and behavior; instances hold individual state.
self refers to the instance receiving a method call.
Choose object-oriented design when it clarifies the problem, not simply because it is available.

modules.title: File Handling & Exceptions
modules.description: Read and write files safely and respond to expected runtime errors.
notes: Use open() with a mode that matches the task; text files commonly use r to read and w to write. The w mode replaces an existing file's contents.
A with statement closes the file automatically, including when an error occurs. Specify encoding="utf-8" for predictable text handling across systems.
Catch specific exceptions around operations that can fail, such as FileNotFoundError. Do not silently swallow errors with a bare except; unexpected failures should remain visible.
modules.code:
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("hello.txt")
path.write_text("Hello, file!", encoding="utf-8")
with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as file:
    text = file.read()
print(text)
takeaways: Use with to manage file resources safely.
Choose file modes carefully; writing with w overwrites existing content.
Handle expected errors specifically and keep useful diagnostic information.

modules.title: Modules & Libraries
modules.description: Organize code into modules and use Python's standard library and installed packages.
notes: A module is a Python file that can define reusable names. import math makes the module available under its name; from math import sqrt imports a particular name.
The standard library ships with Python and provides tested tools for common tasks. Third-party packages must be installed in the environment before they can be imported.
When a file is run directly, __name__ is set to "__main__". A main guard keeps script-only behavior from running when the module is imported.
takeaways: Imports let you reuse code and keep related functionality organized.
Prefer standard-library tools when they fit; install external libraries in the correct environment.
A main guard separates reusable definitions from script entry-point behavior.

modules.title: Projects & Problem Solving
modules.description: Break a small task into manageable steps, test assumptions, and build a useful command-line program.
notes: Start by stating the inputs, expected outputs, and edge cases. Decompose the task into small functions whose names describe their purpose.
Validate external input before using it. Catch a narrow exception such as ValueError when converting user-provided text to a number, and explain the issue clearly.
Test normal cases and boundary cases, then refine the design. For larger projects, add automated tests and keep application logic separate from input/output where practical.
takeaways: Define the problem and edge cases before writing the full solution.
Small functions and clear validation make projects easier to debug.
Test both typical inputs and cases that should fail.

datascience.title: Data Science
datascience.description: An approachable introduction to the data science workflow, trustworthy data, exploration, modeling, and responsible evaluation.

modules.title: The Data Science Workflow
modules.description: Learn how a question becomes a data-backed analysis, and why iteration and context matter.
notes: A typical workflow starts with a decision or question, then collects or accesses relevant data, inspects and prepares it, explores patterns, and communicates results. The steps often repeat as new questions arise.

Define the unit of observation and what each row represents before analyzing a table. A dataset can be technically correct yet unsuitable for the question if its population, time period, or measurements do not match.
Keep a record of data sources, assumptions, and transformations so results can be checked and reproduced. An observed association alone does not establish that one factor caused another.
modules.code:
records = [{"day": "Mon", "visits": 12}, {"day": "Tue", "visits": 15}]
total_visits = sum(row["visits"] for row in records)
print(f"Rows: {len(records)}, total visits: {total_visits}")
takeaways: Begin with a well-defined question and understand what each observation represents.
Data preparation and analysis are iterative, not a one-way checklist.
Record assumptions and avoid interpreting correlation as proof of causation.

modules.title: Data Types & Quality
modules.description: Recognize common data types and inspect missing, inconsistent, or implausible values.
notes: Numeric measurements, categories, dates, text, and identifiers have different meanings. A number used as an ID is usually a label, not a quantity suitable for arithmetic.

Quality checks include missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent units or labels, invalid ranges, and parsing errors. A missing value is not automatically zero, and the right treatment depends on why it is missing and the task.

Clean values without erasing useful information: preserve raw data when possible, document transformations, and verify the result. The small example uses Python's standard library; real tables may use tools such as pandas.
modules.code:
rows = [{"id": "A1", "age": 20}, {"id": "A2", "age": None}, {"id": "A1", "age": 20}]
missing_ages = sum(row["age"] is None for row in rows)
duplicate_rows = len(rows) - len({(row["id"], row["age"]) for row in rows})
print(missing_ages, duplicate_rows)
takeaways: Interpret a field by its meaning, not merely by how it is stored.
Missingness, duplicates, and invalid values require investigation before treatment.
Preserve raw data and document any cleaning decisions.

modules.title: Descriptive Statistics
modules.description: Summarize a numeric sample using center, spread, and a careful look at outliers.
notes: The mean uses every value but can be pulled by extreme observations; the median is the middle after sorting and is often more robust for skewed data. Neither summary replaces inspecting the distribution.
Range and standard deviation describe spread in different ways. Standard deviation is expressed in the original measurement units and can also be sensitive to outliers.
These summaries describe the values provided, not necessarily a wider population. Inference requires attention to sampling design, uncertainty, and assumptions.
modules.code:
from statistics import mean, median, pstdev

values = [2, 4, 4, 10]
print(mean(values), median(values), round(pstdev(values), 2))
takeaways: Use more than one summary to understand center and spread.
The median can better represent a skewed sample, while the mean is sensitive to extremes.
Descriptive statistics alone do not establish population-level conclusions.

modules.title: Visualization
modules.description: Choose a clear chart that matches the question, data type, and audience.
notes: Bar charts compare categories, histograms show the distribution of a numeric variable, and line charts commonly show values across an ordered time axis. Chart choice should follow the question rather than decoration.
Use descriptive titles, axis labels, units, and honest scales. Avoid visual choices that exaggerate differences, and distinguish missing values from true zeros.

This example uses Matplotlib, a widely used third-party library; install it in the active Python environment with pip if needed. In a graphical or notebook environment, show() displays the chart; some servers instead need a saved image.
modules.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
visits = [12, 15, 11]
plt.plot(days, visits, marker="o")
plt.title("Daily visits")
plt.xlabel("Day")
plt.ylabel("Visits")
plt.show()
modules.output: Displays a labeled line chart of visits for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.
takeaways: Match the chart type to the variable and comparison you want to show.
Label axes, units, and context so a chart can be read accurately.
Visualization can reveal patterns but does not by itself explain their causes.

modules.title: Introduction to Supervised Learning
modules.description: Understand features, labels, and a simple regression model that learns from examples.
notes: In supervised learning, examples include features (inputs) and a target label or value to predict. Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numeric values.

A model learns patterns from training data and then applies them to new inputs. A simple model can capture only simple relationships, and a close fit on training examples does not guarantee good performance on unseen data.
This example uses scikit-learn, which must be installed in the active Python environment. Its tiny synthetic dataset demonstrates API mechanics, not a reliable real-world relationship.
modules.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# One feature: hours studied; target: synthetic score.
X = [[1], [2], [3]]
y = [2, 4, 6]
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print(round(model.predict([[4]])[0], 1))
takeaways: Features are inputs and the target is the value or category being predicted.
Train on examples, then assess predictions on data not used for fitting.
A toy dataset teaches the mechanics but cannot justify broad real-world conclusions.

modules.title: Evaluation & Ethics
modules.description: Evaluate predictions carefully and consider fairness, privacy, and consequences of use.
notes: For classification, accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct, but it can hide poor performance on a rare class. Precision, recall, and a confusion matrix can provide additional context; metric choice should reflect the cost of different errors.
Keep evaluation data separate from training data to estimate performance on unseen cases. Repeatedly tuning decisions against the test set can leak information and make the estimate optimistic.

Check whether data and labels reflect historical or sampling biases, protect sensitive information, and consider who may be harmed by errors. Fairness has multiple definitions and trade-offs; a metric alone cannot settle an ethical decision.
modules.code:
actual = [1, 0, 1, 1]
predicted = [1, 0, 0, 1]
correct = sum(a == p for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
accuracy = correct / len(actual)
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
takeaways: Choose evaluation metrics that reflect the task and the consequences of errors.
Use held-out data for an honest check and avoid tuning repeatedly on the test set.
Responsible data science considers privacy, bias, affected people, and limits of the model.
